title: Running a chhabeel
hookLine: set up your own stall of cold sweet water in June
tomorrow: Simran's dad sets lamps at the door every autumn. who are they for?

lines: A HEAT WAVE, A LINE OF CARS.
A COLD CUP, WITH BOTH HANDS.
cards: A long line of cars in a heat wave. Windows down, the air shimmering over the asphalt, and somebody at the curb is waving you toward a folding table. Steel drums, a ladle, a stack of paper cups.

A teenager in a bright scarf hands a cup through the window, something cold and pale and sweet, with both hands. The driver reaches for a wallet. She shakes her head, smiles, and points to the next car.

teach.h: GURU ARJAN'S DAY, IN THE HEAT.
teach.b: That's a chhabeel. Sikhs set them up in the summer heat around the martyrdom day of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru. Tradition says his last days, in a Lahore summer, were hard ones, and that he did not give way.
A line of his in Raag Asa holds the heart of it: teraa keeaa meethaa laagai.
What You do tastes sweet to me. So on his day, Sikhs hand out something sweet and cold, for nothing. Taste is the whole lesson.
The drink is often kachi lassi: water with a little milk and sugar, poured over ice. Three details make it a chhabeel and not a lemonade stand. It's free: no tip jar.
It's for anyone: no one is asked a name or a faith.

teach.h: FREE, FOR ANYONE, WITH BOTH HANDS.
teach.b: And it's given with both hands, the way you'd hand something to a guest you honor.

teach.h: A HARD MEMORY, KEPT AS A JOB.

teach.b: In that heat, a cold cup isn't a snack; it's relief. So the memory of a hard death is kept as a job: standing in the heat, cooling strangers.

how: Around Guru Arjan's martyrdom day, Sikh families and gurdwaras set up chhabeels, free stalls of cold sweetened drink such as kachi lassi, and hand cups to anyone passing, often by the roadside.

o: a free stall of cold sweet water in summer heat
a bake sale that raises money for langar
a tent where the Guru Granth Sahib rests outdoors

games.q: what makes a chhabeel — tap the pairs.
p: water, a little milk, sugar, ice
what You do tastes sweet to me

s: anyone in the heat gets a cup: drivers, kids, strangers. no name or faith asked.
the drink is often kachi lassi: water, a little milk, sugar and ice
pale, sweet and cold, ladled from steel drums.
a chhabeel is a fundraiser for the gurdwara
it's free. no tip jar, no price.

games.q: a man in a work truck drinks a cup, then asks if he should donate something, since he isn't Sikh. what do you say?
o: no need: it's free, for anyone, and nobody's asking who you are.
a small donation is polite, since he isn't part of the sangat.
it's free for Sikhs; others usually drop something in the jar.
games.why: a chhabeel is free and for anyone, handed over with both hands. that's how Guru Arjan's day is kept: cooling strangers, no questions.

practice: If there's a glass of water near you, hold it in both hands first and feel how cool it is. Take one slow sip and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow, then breathe, and sip again when you're ready.
If there's no glass, remember the last cold drink someone handed you, and taste it again in memory.

wordCard.voice: Running a chhabeel. Setting up a stall of cold, sweet water, free to anyone, in the summer heat of Guru Arjan's martyrdom day.

orig.note: Punjabi: a free stall of cold, sweet drink set up in the summer heat.

carryVoice: For the road: cold water, freely, with both hands and no questions asked. Day 1754, ice still clinking.
